title: 40% of what you learned is gone in 20 minutes

caption.kern: A German psychologist memorized nonsense syllables by the thousand, alone in his study, just to time how fast his own memory failed him. Turns out most of it was gone before the day was over. 🧠⏳
caption.detail: Hermann Ebbinghaus ran the experiment on himself in 1885, using the "savings method" — relearning lists and measuring how much faster it went the second time. His curve showed roughly 40% forgotten after 20 minutes, 56% after an hour, and up to 70% within 24 hours without review. A 2015 replication using modern methods found the same shape.
caption.kontext: The forgetting isn't the interesting part — the reset is. One review, even a short one, doesn't just buy you a few more hours. It flattens the whole curve. That's the entire case against cramming.
caption.frage: When did you last look at something you "already know" — on purpose?
caption.sources: Sources: Ebbinghaus, H. — Über das Gedächtnis, 1885 • Murre, J.M.J. & Dros, J. — Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve • PLoS ONE 10(7): e0120644, July 2015 • doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0120644
